articles.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. Yalta ratified — but did not create — the division of Europe into spheres of influence that later became frozen into the dividing lines of the Cold War. A less apoplectic strain of the same underlying sentiment holds that President Trump’s willingness to meet his Russian and Chinese counterparts is in itself an unnecessary concession to Russia and China that merely signals weakness and does nothing to advance U.S. interests; as if the avoidance of nuclear war with China were not a vital U.S. interest. The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands . articles.title: "Now We Have The Answer": Retrial Jury Convicts Man Who Sparked Palisades Inferno
articles.description: "Now We Have The Answer": Retrial Jury Convicts Man Who Sparked Palisades Inferno Authored by Beige Luciano-Adams via The Epoch Times , LOS ANGELES - After deliberating for less than two days, a Los Angeles jury unanimously found a federal arson suspect guilty of lighting a brush fire in the Santa Monica Mountains that would lead, days later, to the catastrophic Palisades Fire of 2025 . The retrial of Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, began Nov. 4 after jurors in a first trial deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal in June , leading U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang to declare a mistrial . Rinderknecht, a dual U.S.-French citizen, pleaded not guilty to a revised indictment charging him with two counts of federal arson related to damage to federal property and property used in interstate commerce. The jury on Nov. 20 found him guilty on both counts. Sentencing in the case is set for March 17, 2027. The charges carry a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and a combined statutory maximum of 40 years. Investigators alleged that the defendant on Jan. 1 ignited a brush fire, dubbed the Lachman Fire, which smoldered underground for a week until reemerging to the surface through a single shrub.

articles.description: Ukraine Strikes Commercial Vessel In Gulf Of Finland In War First On Saturday a Russian ship has been struck in the Gulf of Finland, with major rescue efforts underway hours after the attack, with the cargo ship on fire and drifting . The ship, the Sparta II, was reportedly hit by drones close to Russia's maritime border , but has now drifted into Finnish territorial waters . Ukraine is of course the main suspect at this time, though the precise origin of the drones has not been initially confirmed. articles.title: Jeffrey Sachs: Europe Chooses Wrong Security Architecture
articles.description: Jeffrey Sachs: Europe Chooses Wrong Security Architecture Authored by Jeffrey D. Sachs Russia has called for a new European security architecture for nearly two decades, beginning with President Vladimir Putin’s Munich speech in 2007 and President Dmitri Medvedev’s proposed European Security Treaty in 2008, followed by Moscow’s draft treaties of December 2021 and Putin’s call in June 2024 for indivisible security across Eurasia. The Western reply has not changed. As a British statement to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) put it in June 2026, Russia keeps calling for a new security architecture, “but we already have one . ” Britain’s account is false. Europe has not one security architecture but two, built on incompatible premises. The first is the OSCE, which includes every state from Vancouver to Vladivostok and rests on indivisible security, the principle that no state should strengthen its security at the expense of others . This is the Golden Rule applied to nations. The second is NATO , a U.S.-led alliance premised on Western predominance and military superiority over Russia. The OSCE is an architecture of international law and mutual restraint.

articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records
articles.description: Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years. Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. articles.title: Dashing through the snow: 10 of the UK’s best Christmas train rides

From your first-class carriage of either a steam-hauled or heritage diesel engine, you will be served sandwiches and cakes from traditional tiered plates, washed down with hot drinks and fizz. Santa and his elves will visit your carriage with presents for children, otherwise sit back and enjoy the woodland and moorland scenery of rural Speyside on this 20-mile round-trip (lasting about 1 hour and 40 minutes) between Aviemore and Broomhill. Weekends and select weekdays until 24 December, £260 for four people . Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

More importantly, it’s fantastic: you might call it trip-hop were Sinéad O’Connor’s vocal not so intense as to negate any potential for relaxation on the part of the listener. Continue reading...

articles.title: I’m engaged but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel? | Leading questions
articles.description: Telling him would risk a lot of harm, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. If you’re going to take that gamble, you’d better be sure why you’re doing it Read more Leading questions My partner and I are engaged after a whirlwind romance, and I was over the moon when he proposed. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings. Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
articles.description: Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities • Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh . The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap. Emily Continue reading...

articles.description: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
articles.description: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. articles.title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships
articles.description: Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change . I have spoken to people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s, describing age gaps far greater than three years; often with people twice their age or more. It’s noticeable that social norms and taboos didn’t change hugely between the start of the 1960s and the end of the 80s; in most cases, their pare

articles.title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
articles.description: (CDR) Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion. Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling lat

articles.title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
articles.description: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his

articles.title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’
articles.description: The American novelist on the wild side of Maurice Sendak, re-evaluating Gone With the Wind, and the magical comforts of Alice Hoffman My favourite book growing up I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me. The book that changed me as a teenager A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living. Continue reading...

articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. articles.title: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means
articles.description: Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit Cop31 live – latest updates The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilateralism and resolves to remain united in the pursuit of efforts to implement the Convention and achieve the purpose and long-term goals of the Paris Agreement; 2. articles.title: Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?
articles.description: Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world . On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg). People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
articles.description: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than incr

articles.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
articles.description: A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026 , but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck ’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it , even given their extravagant headgear. A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in

articles.title: We should be free to call ourselves Black English | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article about categories on the census form It’s about time we fixed the Black English category in the census, whether popular or not ( It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose, 14 November ). Categories count. They make citizens, politically engineer belonging and allow people to be seen and to see themselves. The excuse that the Black English category is simply unpopular doesn’t wash. I remember in the 1990s when the Black British, or Black African categories were all the rage, they were never particularly comfortable to tick, but we all got over ourselves and stomached the flattening of our complex identities for what we believed was a good cause. A Black English category would also help me out enormously, living as I do in France, where people don’t believe me when I say I’m English, but simply think I’m deluded and can’t speak French properly – which I can. Having left Scotland when I was three and grown up in London, I felt I couldn’t legitimately call myself Scottish – but English, I could. Years ago I stopped calling myself Britannique , because Black or otherwise, it just didn’t reall

articles.title: Judges, juries and rape myths in trials | Letters
articles.description: Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham In your report ( ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November ), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind. It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters
articles.description: Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas Rachel Dixon’s article ( The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November ) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around  £1,000 a year , and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten. It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters
articles.description: Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter “Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments ( Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November ). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation. It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told that “it’s fine”, but as a long-Covid sufferer for 2.5 years, I can tell you this disease is vile: I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy, certainly not my loved ones. I am unable to go for a walk, be social or stay active. If people feel ill (even “just a cold”) they should stay at home and avoid spreading their germs to everyone they meet, because they probably won’t know who is vulnerable. Sally Billenness Hounslow, London

articles.title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash
articles.description: Young Vic, London Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama. Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio. Continue reading...

articles.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
articles.description: Isaac Eiger’s solo venture leaves jangle pop behind for a wilder sound. Often it owes a debt to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days? From New York via Montana Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children). Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. articles.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup

The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. articles.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
articles.description: Hepworth Wakefield, West Yorkshire He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable. It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.” Continue reading...

He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet. Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. (It was originally made for Milwaukee Ballet, where Pink has been artistic director since 2002.) Continue reading...

It’s very sweet – but the storylines and supporting characters are flimsy to say the least Bill Beam (Rob Brydon) is a chump, a sap, a bejumpered limpet clinging to the peripheries of his own existence. “I’m being left behind,” he tells best friend Drew (Kevin Eldon) who, having heard this – and that, and the other – a thousand times before, stifles a well-earned yawn. Bill’s wife has left him for the gardener (“No hard feelings!”) and lo, this ever-dimming bulb of cable-knit neediness must find a solution to both his newfound “cashflow crisis” and deepening existential haplessness. articles.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
articles.description: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. Continue reading...

The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has broken the £100 barrier , and some of the packets look smaller than they were. But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded. articles.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
articles.description: For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful? • This article does not contain major spoilers Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there . Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding. Continue reading...

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity. articles.title: Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days
articles.description: Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter. The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The platonic ideal of a wine glass’: we test the best for every budget
articles.description: Searching for a wine glass that can do it all? From short-stemmed to swirlable, dishwasher-friendly to delicate, here’s the glassware that’s a cut above the rest • The best no- and low-alcohol wines for when you’re off the booze It is a truth only sometimes acknowledged that wine is in want of a good drinking vessel. Why? Because wine experts agree that the shape, character and feel of a glass give wine the conditions to shine. “A good glass can greatly improve your experience,” writes David Williams in The Encyclopedia of Wine . He adds that expense isn’t necessary: “[A]s a rule, the thinner the glass the better, while an oval shape and generous (but not enormous) bowl are best at capturing and releasing a wine’s flavours.” Drinking wine is an experience beyond flavour; before the taste, there is the nose, and a good glass will amplify its aromas. Likewise, there is the ineffable question of how a wine makes us feel; again, your choice of glass feeds into this experience – how does it feel to hold, to swirl, to sip from? Continue reading...

This means you can watch Mary Berry avidly talk about the joy of eating mince pies, followed by a Christmas-themed murder in the Caribbean in Death in Paradise, well before the tree is up (unless, of course, you put up your tree earlier than ever, too). articles.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
articles.description: The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.” Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy. articles.title: The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same | Gordon Brown
articles.description: As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France , Poland , Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism. Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states . Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east , Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south. Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 Continue reading...

articles.title: Why is Shabana Mahmood tackling ‘two-tier policing’ if she doesn’t believe it exists? | Gaby Hinsliff
articles.description: Is it the home secretary’s job to act tough addressing a rightwing myth or to face it down? She seems to have chosen the path of least resistance Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr. But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic. Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City | Imogen West-Knights
articles.description: Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu . You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto , the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal? Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run. articles.title: Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago | Kayode Akintola
articles.description: The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease . That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying . There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths . The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?
articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind. Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. Whatever your preferred publication, left or right, high- or lowbrow, it will have proffered its own take on the game, whether it’s to bemoan its godless influence on adolescent men or to laud its u

articles.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for almond sorbet with grape granita
articles.description: This dessert makes me feel like I’m in Sicily again Ice-cream holds an irresistible allure for me. That combination of richness, lightness, and the pure, sensual pleasure of it melting gently across the palate maintains an unbreakable hold over my imagination. In fact, other than fruit, it’s the only sweet food with which I have a genuine emotional relationship: I can remember many ice-creams I’ve eaten incredibly vividly, and in a way I just don’t with almost all other desserts and pastries. Today’s ice is a case in point, having been developed from a memory of an almond gelato eaten in Sicily just after the annual harvest. Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London Continue reading...

articles.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
articles.description: Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands. That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns ( lussekatter ) replaces cinnamon buns for fika , our revered tradition of coffee and cake. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall
articles.description: Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider ( Araneus diadematus ) outside our back window. Is that a smile? Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived nearby. Contemporary experiments with honeybees have shown that diversity in workers’ personality traits makes for an adaptable and resilient hive. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the uncharted trauma of breaking up with AI companions
articles.description: People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away. “It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
articles.description: When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement? What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.” Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind. Continue reading...

articles.title: SNL’s skit Sister captures the quiet agony of caregiving for women: ‘I’ve never felt seen like that’
articles.description: The viral satirization of the caregiving burden left to women and daughters hit home for many viewers The Saturday Night Live sketch , titled Sister quickly went viral this week for its satirization of the burden that women and daughters face to take care of aging family members. In the parody commercial, comedian John Mulaney touts the benefit of “Sister”, who he describes as “a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister” . “Now I don’t have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do,” Mulaney says, as the sister, played by cast member Jane Wickline, gives their father’s medication to him. The sketch, which amassed over seven million views on YouTube in less than a week since it aired, has received thousands of responses and comments about its accuracy. “This is one of the MOST wicked and spot on SNL sketches ever written,” wrote one commenter on YouTube. Another posted: “As a hospice nurse this definitely tracks. I deal 90% of the time with adult daughters, and if there is no daughter, it is the daughter in law.” “This is so real it almost ga

articles.title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers
articles.description: A heatwave in the Bering Sea that killed 10bn snow crabs has led to a new hybrid emerging that has no fishing quotas Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong. The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species. Continue reading...

articles.title: Richard Hammond: ‘I’m much taller than you think. I’m just standing further away’
articles.description: The TV presenter on his costly divorce, his ‘stupid’ hair, and why his driving licence is on life support Born in Solihull, West Midlands, Richard Hammond, 56, attended Harrogate College of Art and Technology and began his broadcasting career in local radio. He went on to become a presenter for the Men & Motors TV channel and, from 2002 to 2015, he was part of the BBC’s Top Gear team with Jeremy Clarkson and James May. In 2016, the trio started to host The Grand Tour for Amazon Prime. Since 2021, Hammond has presented the restoration programme, Richard Hammond’s Workshop, which is in its sixth season and available on Quest. He is divorced with two daughters and lives in Monmouthshire, Wales. When were you happiest? Whenever I’m either walking on a mountain fell, or on a motorcycle. Continue reading...

articles.title: Slade helps sparkling England power to record victory as All Blacks wilt again
articles.description: England 37-12 New Zealand Slade scores the first of five tries for England Every year the All Blacks come to south-west London it feels like an acid test. And rarely, if ever, have England responded with such class and conviction on this famous old stretch of grass. New Zealand simply could not live with their clear-eyed, motivated opponents who, at times, made their illustrious visitors look horribly second-rate. If Kiwi fans thought last week’s loss to Wales was painful this was arguably as bad in terms of the reputational damage. The home side were 19-0 up after 36 minutes and had the game all but wrapped up within a couple of minutes of the restart when Ollie Chessum smashed his way over to claim his side’s fourth try. In terms of England’s margin of victory, this was New Zealand’s heaviest loss to any northern hemisphere nation in their proud history. Continue reading...

articles.description: All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’ The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said. articles.description: Thursday’s byelection in Castle Bromwich will be latest test for Nigel Farage’s party as rival eats into support Voters go to the polls in the village of Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands on Thursday in a little-noticed election that is the latest test for Reform at a time when it is particularly vulnerable. articles.title: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
articles.description: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out. Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape
articles.description: Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said. In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”. Continue reading...

The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence. articles.title: Deniz Tek: ‘Top Gun may have got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman from me’

When I was in the US Marines F-4 Phantom squadron, Iceman was my call sign, which is given to you on your first operational deployment. You have it on your helmet and a patch on your flight suit. One day, a film crew came to visit our squadron, doing research for a film they were working on, and they hung out with us for two weeks. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Music was our teacher’: the sound system pioneers reviving the scene in Manchester and beyond
articles.description: Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the history lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms, but through towering stacks of amps and speakers, turntables and Jamaican records. “We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley, Culture, that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. For us, the sound system was not just entertainment – it was an education.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Alcaraz holds off Shelton to set up final showdown with Zverev at ATP Finals
articles.description: Spaniard beats American 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (1) in semi-final Alexander Zverev sees off Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4 The man himself was not present in Turin on Saturday afternoon, but one of the most intriguing developments on and off court in men’s tennis this year was Ben Shelton’s surprise decision to hire the former world No 1 Juan Carlos Ferrero as his new coach alongside his father, Bryan. Ferrero is one of the most highly respected coaches on tour, but he also knows Carlos Alcaraz better than any other coach in the world. However, there is only so much that anyone can do against one of the sport’s greatest talents. Shelton, the third seed, played a spectacular match, serving monstrously, attacking without hesitation and volleying well in decisive moments, but it still wasn’t enough to defeat the second seeded Alcaraz, who maintained his focus after an uncertain start as he reached the final of the ATP Finals with a 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (1) win. articles.title: WSL roundup: Chelsea thwarted by Liverpool keeper, London City move to third
articles.description: Keating’s resilience keeps Chelsea at bay in 0-0 draw Van de Donk and Putellas score twice to sink Palace 6-2 Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea , the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point, while London City Lionesses moved to within four points of the top by beating Crystal Palace 6-2. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night , Chelsea drew a blank. Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after they beat City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short. articles.title: Fiona the hippo’s death was tragic. But blaming a ‘bad mom’ is absurd | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: The beloved animal died after ingesting a hat. Some are seeking a scapegoat – and we’ve heard this story before “Do they know the identity of the mother of the boy with the hat Fiona swallowed??” asks one Facebook post with thousands of likes. “She should be charged!!” Spend a few minutes scrolling social media, and you will find endless variations of this statement. On Thursday, Fiona, a beloved hippo , died after eating a hat that had fallen into her enclosure at the Cincinnati zoo. Now a lot of angry people are out for blood. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Dismantling patriarchy: An evening of conversation, art and resistance. On Monday 1 March 2027, join Arwa Mahdawi and One Billion Rising as we bring together activists and artists to question patriarchy, power, and celebrate resistance. What would a world beyond patriarchy look like? And what will it take to get there? Book tickets here or at guardian.live Continue reading...

articles.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
articles.description: Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. Continue reading...

articles.title: US pursuit of ‘Trump-class’ warships has blown cost of new fleet by billions, report warns
articles.description: Iran war stretching fleet’s capacity, navy chief admits, as CBO finds estimated cost of new ships ‘unrealistically low’ The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity. The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer. Continue reading...

articles.title: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
articles.description: Foreign combatants in Port-au-Prince welcomed by many after years of gang control but some fear offensive could exacerbate volatile situation A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch. In 2024, as the surrounding city was almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs , Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad . Continue reading...

articles.title: Mark Carney is so popular he can get away with a lot. Will it last if the Trump spell breaks?
articles.description: Canadians have put a lot of trust in their prime minister but some question if it can last if the trade wars were to end In the hours after polls in the US midterm elections closed and it became clear that Donald Trump had been rebuked in historic fashion, Canadian politicians were elated. “I was doing cartwheels down the street, and have you ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels?” said Ontario premier Doug Ford, a prominent critic of American tariffs. Continue reading...

articles.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
articles.description: Experts say BBLs and other cosmetic procedures can be risky and seasonal offers at clinics in England could make people rush decisions Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure. The government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs , vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
articles.description: M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra. Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but

articles.title: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80
articles.description: Director and Scorsese collaborator is using AI in films and sees its takeover as inevitable, not just in cinema Paul Schrader was sipping white wine in a Greenwich Village trattoria when he said how he felt about using AI to make films: “I am opening the cage of a monster and I don’t have a leash.” The 80-year-old film-maker behind Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and American Gigolo, is embracing the technology as he enters the final act of a prolific career in which he has collaborated with Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro, Sigourney Weaver and Richard Gere. Continue reading...

articles.title: Promise Me, America by Joe Biden review – former president defends his decisions
articles.description: New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party. Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election. Continue reading...

articles.title: A Robbie Williams film starring a CGI chimp helped me come to terms with my hearing loss
articles.description: I was bullied for my deafness as a child, and just when I was finding myself, a car crash set me back years. But then I watched the movie Better Man, and had my life explained for me I cannot say I’ve ever been a Robbie Williams fan. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life. I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. I was a misfit in my family, with no support for my deafness, and at school the bullying – from kids and teachers – was something awful. In my desperate isolation, I turned to reading: book reading, lip-reading, and reading the room. Forget TV, forget music – the Beano andBeezer were my survival manuals: the Numskulls taught me how my brain worked with broken ears. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Napping together on the reeds, the swans appeared luminous’: Noah Forster’s best phone picture
articles.description: The photographer hopes his intimate photograph of two sleeping birds will remind others of their special person Twenty-one-year-old Noah Forster had always thought swans were beautiful, but it was his girlfriend Cecilia is the one who made him really notice them. The pair began dating two years ago, but now live 70 miles apart; he is a welder in Newark-on-Trent, she is studying law in Leeds. “The distance can be difficult, but we try to talk as much as possible,” Forster says. “It’s taken me a while to save up for a driver’s licence and car, so I have a daily walk from my home and across the River Trent to get the 6am train to work. We like to send photos of our day to each other, and I took this photo on an exceptionally cold and frosty morning in November, walking across the river to get to work. I saw these swans near the castle. Napping together on the reeds, they appeared luminous.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
articles.description: Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction. After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Bland, faintly sugary and cardboardy’: the best (and worst) supermarket porridge oats, tasted and rated
articles.description: Which get the day off to a satisfying start – and which make for a gruelling breakfast? • The best supermarket natural yoghurts In the winter of 2003-04, my girlfriend and I hosted a Scottish family at a chalet in Val d’Isère. Full of chef bravado, I promised the father that I’d make him the best bowl of breakfast porridge he’d ever had. He, of course, turned up his nose at my bowl of sweet dessert, which I’d laced with cream and sugar, and showed me how to make porridge with just water and salt instead. I’ve never looked back. In my experience, most jumbo oats need twice as much water as the packet instructions suggest, as well as three times as long to cook and turn satisfyingly creamy. Regular and vigorous stirring is essential, too, as is the sea salt, which turns a bland bowl of pap into a naturally sweet, earthy and nutty porridge. Continue reading...

articles.title: Vienna on a plate: a food lover’s guide to the Austrian capital
articles.description: Some of the city’s best chefs, Ola Szwarc, Nadim Amin, Konstantin Filippou and Felix Mandl, share their favourite cafes, bars and restaurants There are two sides to coffee in Vienna. The grand, old-school coffee houses are incredible places to sit, have breakfast, drink a beer and forget about time. They have much the same function as a pub in Britain. For that experience, we’d go to Café Prückel or Café Hawelka . For a quintessential Viennese coffee, we’d suggest a wiener melange – somewhat similar to a cappuccino, but traditionally a little milder, made with coffee, steamed milk and milk foam. Alternatively, an einspänner is another peculiar, old-fashioned option: a strong black coffee served in a glass with a layer of cold whipped cream on top. If we want good coffee that actually wakes us up, we go to Kaffeemodul . You can choose the style you like, from fruity to less fruity. NA Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna’
articles.description: There’s more to the Austrian capital’s cuisine than schnitzel – its dishes come from all over the world The Viennese love to eat. That isn’t solely a sign of joie de vivre. Sometimes it’s just hunger. The city has a long history of decline. Entire empires have crumbled here, or simply dissolved. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles. Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. articles.description: If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park. Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.
