articles.title: Wales fightback not enough as Australia edge thriller thanks to Gordon
articles.description: Wales 26-29 Australia Wales to face Japan in ninth-place final One step at a time. Historic victories are one thing, but the boring need to back up such a win proved beyond Wales. Cardiff was rocking. A few thousand short of capacity the stadium may have been, but 66,000 rocked it as of yore. Wales’s young side could not quite respond. This was a reverse of last weekend’s win against New Zealand . In the first half, in particular, Wales’s dominance was all but total, but like the All Blacks, they just could not make it tell. Australia had the lead at the break and in a more open second half they proved just as deadly. Thus they claim their place in the fifth-place final at Twickenham, where they will face Ireland on Friday night. Wales must make do with a ninth-placed final against Japan on Saturday. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Fragile’ Chelsea must toughen up after Leeds humiliation, admits Xabi Alonso
articles.description: Xabi Alonso is straying towards crisis territory. Here’s a mind-bending statistic: Chelsea are eighth but have now lost more league games than Manchester United. They were bullied by a rampant Leeds United, who fully merited their first win at Stamford Bridge since going top with a 2-0 victory in December 1999, and can look forward to another season with no European football if they do not sharpen up soon. It is not really worth dwelling on the fact that the second Leeds goal, a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty converted early in an astonishingly one-sided second half, came after Morgan Rogers was harshly penalised for handball. That was a minor detail given the wider picture. Leeds, superbly coached by Daniel Farke and up to sixth after two clinical strikes from Noah Okafor, Calvert-Lewin’s sixth goal of the season and a late effort from Brenden Aaronson, were so dominant that they had no real need for a helping hand from the officials. Continue reading...

articles.title: Aston Villa held at home as dogged Sunderland battle for Régis Le Bris
articles.description: For Aston Villa , a painful stalemate at home to Sunderland, but for Régis Le Bris and his players, this was another triumph of sorts. The raw numbers spoke volumes of Villa’s struggles against a defence that backed themselves to keep Unai Emery’s side at bay. All but one of Villa’s seven shots on target came from outside the visitors’ box and the one inside it, courtesy of Ian Maatsen, was forgettable. Owing to a summer of change, injuries and Emery resting John McGinn with Tuesday’s game at Galatasaray in mind, Maatsen, incredibly, was the sole survivor in the Villa starting XI from when these sides played out a 4-3 classic seven months ago. Villa were too predictable, short of a spark, someone to unpick an organised back line. Johan Manzambi, Emi Buendía and Alysson all flattered to deceive on an afternoon when Ibrahim Mbaye and McGinn arrived from the bench. Alejandro Garnacho, however, was not involved in Villa’s matchday squad for the second successive match and the Chelsea loanee has played just 38 minutes in the Premier League this campaign. Tammy Abraham, the match-winner in April, was also left out and a January move looks likely. Continue reading...

Sabah Kerjota and Pierre Landry Kaboré both scored twice with Claudio Braga, Sabri Guendouz, Stuart Findlay and a Ryan Finnigan own goal completing the rout. articles.title: Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson
articles.description: Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation. Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager. Continue reading...

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.description: Crooke Claims CIA Was Behind Kerch Bridge Strike As Pentagon Says Deep Strikes Fail Former British diplomat Alastair Crooke says the strike that dropped a span of the Kerch Bridge was no Ukrainian solo act. "It seemed to have been coordinated by an aircraft," he told retired Army Lt. Col. Daniel Davis on the latest episode of Daniel Davis Deep Dive , "an American aircraft that coordinated the signal." Illustration of the collapsed Kerch Bridge road span, adapted from archival photographs by Rosavtodor.ru ( CC BY 4.0 ) and U.S. Air Force. He put the missiles at "about nine," and pointed to the Dutch firm that makes them, which has publicly taken credit for the hit. That firm is Destinus, which said seven of its Ruta cruise missiles hit the crossing on the second day of strikes, collapsing a span . articles.description: 10 Ways Americans Endured The Great Depression, And Why Today We're Completely Unprepared Authored by John Walter via Substack , Seventeen thousand veterans camped on the Anacostia flats in the summer of 1932, most of them with wives and children, waiting on a bonus Congress had promised for 1945 and then offered early and then withdrew. Shacks went up out of packing crates and scrap. Cavalry and six tanks cleared the camps at the end of July, gas first, then fire, and the shacks burned through the night; two veterans died of it. The Bonus Army went home to nothing, and a country that had already watched nine thousand banks fail got a look at what its own government would do once the patience ran out . Four years earlier the trouble had looked like a stock market problem, something confined to men in hats on Wall Street. Banks went first, then farms, then the factory towns, until twelve and a half million people stood idle and a quarter of the workforce had nothing to sell but its hands. articles.description: Pepe Escobar Predicts Putin Vows 'Massive' Retaliation Over Crimean Bridge Attack, China Quietly Shipping Weapons Material To Iran Via Pakistan Hours after Trump, Xi and Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, Pepe Escobar claimed from the summit city that China is sending "very sensitive weaponizing or electronic material" to Iran by way of Pakistan , and relayed Putin's verdict on the Crimean Bridge strikes: no negotiation, only retaliation. " There is a direct alignment between Beijing, Islamabad and Tehran ," Escobar told Dialogue Works host Nima Rostami Alkhorshid on Thursday. "But Beijing is in the background, everything that they want to happen, it's channeled via Pakistan, including the Chinese sending very sensitive weaponizing or electronic material to Iran." He added: "This goes via Pakistan. Never directly from China. They always have plausible deniability." Muscaro via The Epoch Times , For the first time in human history, an interstellar spacecraft has journeyed a full light-day away from Earth . Voyager 1 left Earth from Florida's Space Coast on Sept. 5, 1977, on a mission to Jupiter, Saturn, and, ultimately, interstellar space, reaching its current speed of 38,000 mph. At 5:16:07 a.m. ET on Nov. 18, 2026, it crossed a threshold of 16 billion miles away from home - a distance that takes light a full 24 hours to travel. "Voyager 1 is exploration at its best," Eric Christian of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center told The Epoch Times. "You build something and you send it out into the unknown, and ... articles.title: Blade Runner 2099: fans will have no idea what is happening in this sci-fi sequel. Why is it even on TV?
articles.description: If you’re a cyberpunk who loves ennui and watching actors you can’t see speak words you can’t hear, get stuck in! The rest of us will just be baffled and bored Why is James Bond not a TV series by now? Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Alien, Star Wars – all given the TV treatment. Franchise-mining is fantastic business, maximising attention share in order to sell adverts. So why not Bond, which is co-owned by Amazon? Maybe watching a punchy sex addict every week, saying his name with weirdly administrative syntax, might just be … too much? I entertained these thoughts while struggling to get through another series expansion: Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, from Wednesday). I’m a fan of the films. Before the original, cinema had imagined the future as serene and orderly. Blade Runner introduced many of us to novelist Philip K Dick’s vision, in which tech has colonised every aspect of life, but inequality has got worse. Surveillance, artificial beings and unchecked corporate power hollow out whatever remains of society. (The fact the new series is on Amazon is the closest it gets to making a joke.) Continue reading...

articles.title: Coventry edge thriller to keep Crystal Palace bottom and ruin Thomas Frank’s start
articles.description: Twice Crystal Palace equalised. They seemed to have stabilised after half-time. But when the momentum is against you, sometimes even a change of manager cannot stop the rot. With five minutes remaining, a long throw arced into the box. Brandon Thomas-Asante headed it goalwards. Dean Henderson got in the way but the ball bounced off him, hit Dwight McNeil and ricocheted in. Palace may feel themselves unlucky, but Thomas Frank started with a defeat and his side have now lost five successive league games. For much of the second half, there had been reasons for Palace optimism. They seemed to have settled better after a ludicrous first half in which neither side looked at all capable of defending. articles.title: Will Apple Charge Rent To Every Agent?
articles.description: Will Apple Charge Rent To Every Agent? Authored by Patrick Feeley via Substack, This afternoon the headlines ran that Apple is working on its own AI agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic and that it has outlined plans for a proactive agent in its job postings. Bloomberg reported that Apple is building an autonomous assistant that can carry out tasks on a user's behalf , that it has considered introducing it as soon as the end of next year, and that development is still at an early stage. Photo by Omid Armin on Unsplash I read the postings, the developer documentation, the earnings call and the court record on the App Store. Apple will ship an agent, and it will be polished, private and permission gated. The larger story is what Apple will do to everyone else's agents. Apple has always charged rent. When Apple announced the App Store on March 6, 2008, Steve Jobs said, as Macworld reported that day, "We don't intend to make any money off the App Store," and the store opened that July with a 30 percent cut. articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green mo

The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. articles.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
articles.description: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suz

articles.description: Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century , that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous cheating; what could they do in the face of such authentic genius? Over and above football matters, it’s clear to see that there were bigger things at stake. Rather obviously, it happened only four years after the Falklands war, which thoroughly poisoned already tense relations between Britain and Argentina. The Match si

articles.title: Chia pudding, pickle and picky dog food: whose fridge is this?
articles.description: ‘Elbow noodles’ for a pet? Obsessed with labels, and jam-packed with condiments, it could only be author and chef Carla Lalli … Cheese I pretty much always have parm or grana padano, and pecorino, for pasta, Caesar salad or a dressing. I’ll have a parmesan rind in the mix, too, for when I’m cooking beans or grains. Then, there’s snacking cheese: sliced cheddar, Pepper Jack or muenster from the deli section for a quesadilla when Cosmo [Lalli’s son] gets home. I love mozzarella sticks for a protein snack, or sometimes when I’m alone, I’ll melt them on stir-fried rice with kimchi, or Korean rice cakes. I always have them in the summer when I go to the beach, too. Marge’s food This is my dog’s food. The usual recipe is a mix of ground minced turkey, minced beef, chicken liver, chicken gizzards, carrot, butternut squash, some frozen kale or spinach, elbow noodles and rice. I truly did not think I would ever be this person, but she’s so picky about her food … I wonder why! But I did get sick of buying food and her leaving half of it behind. Continue reading...

articles.title: Garden composting may not be glamorous, but it brings rich rewards
articles.description: It’s hardly the most exciting aspect of gardening, but getting stuck in now will leave you reaping the benefits in the new year I am going to do the thing that put me off every gardening book I read for the first few years of teaching myself how to garden, and smugly lecture about the importance of soil. But I thought it would be less painful in late November, that languid hinterland between the crisp crunch of bright autumn and the mania of Christmas. If you’d rather, I could bang on about tool-cleaning? Thought not. I am currently evolving into my next method of composting and getting proper compost bays. When we moved in, we inherited a couple of tall plastic bins – or “Daleks” as my fellow columnist Claire Ratinon calls them. Considering I’ve paid very little attention to the compost for the past 15 months, aside from throwing all of our raw fruit and vegetable waste in there, along with leaves and some cardboard, they’ve coped admirably. Continue reading...

articles.title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
articles.description: The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire. But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company. Continue reading...

articles.title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
articles.description: From predatory male celebrities to ordinary men who connive to abuse women, there is no doubt where the problem lies – and the solution too The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men. That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. articles.title: Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet
articles.description: The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality. He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session. Continue reading...

articles.description: After a humiliating NBA finals defeat, the 22-year-old has returned with a vengeance – and the Spurs look like contenders again It wouldn’t be exactly right to say Victor Wembanyama didn’t miss a beat after a disastrous NBA finals in June that left him and his San Antonio Spurs defeated, memed and embarrassed. In the Spurs’ first game this season, against an Oklahoma City Thunder team since decimated by injuries, Wemby went an appalling 1-for-13 from the field. Ten of his 12 points came via free throws. After getting blocked by Aday Mara, he leaned over his knees and muttered furiously to himself as if trying to exorcise an intrusive thought. It brought to mind an image from the NBA finals a few months earlier: Wemby on the floor after being fouled by the Knicks’ Mitchell Robinson, crowing, “I’m in your head!” The Spurs went on to blow a 29-point lead , lose the game and the finals. Now Wemby seemed too preoccupied with the issues within his own dome to worry about wreaking havoc in anybody else’s. articles.title: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
articles.description: Was it all a dream? Has Bond been in hiding? Or will Robert Pattinson simply report to HR on his first day? Russell T Davies, David Hare and more give their takes “James Bond will return,” says the closing title on No Time to Die, the most recent James Bond film and the final one to star Daniel Craig. It is just as well: Bond has to all appearances been vaporised by sea-launched missiles, having been infected by nanobots programmed to attack his nearest and dearest at the slightest touch. No one would believe that one of the world’s most successful film series would come to such an abrupt halt, but no doubt a little reassurance helped. Nevertheless, the first order of business for scriptwriter Steven Knight and director Denis Villeneuve will be dealing with it: how to revive and re-energise a character at the heart of the action. Speculation on their best way forward has been rife, and previous examples are not hard to find. articles.title: England and New Zealand collide with final spots and reputations on the line
articles.description: Discipline, bench impact and the breakdown will be pivotal in what home captain Maro Itoje says is a ‘massive game’ In the brave new world of the Nations Championship things are not as black and white as they used to be. articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.description: The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam ’s version? AwapBamBoogers No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards. articles.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
articles.description: Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases. According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK , fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard. articles.title: Terror on Bondi Beach review – these astounding stories recreate every single second of horror
articles.description: From agonised parents trying to find their children, to the man who tackled a gunman – these gripping accounts of the 2025 Sydney attacks should never be forgotten Milo Riley-Smith’s documentary is a simple piece of diligent work. It begins by spending a short time gathering the backstories of its interviewees: how they or their parents came to Australia seeking a new life, finding it to be a welcoming place where, as one woman remembers, Jews “could have a fair go” because anyone could, whatever their ethnicity. These Jewish Australians then talk about how, after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, they began to feel less safe. They had seen a flaring of antisemitic violence, vandalism and rhetoric; they attended the annual Hanukah festivities at Sydney’s Bondi beach with some trepidation. After an extended account of the events of 14 December 2025, the documentary’s participants comment briefly on whether enough was done by the Australian authorities to protect them. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
articles.description: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. articles.title: From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK | Klaus Brinkbäumer
articles.description: As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back Dear British friends, Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja . Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing. Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany Continue reading...

articles.title: Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest
articles.description: Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter. But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
articles.description: In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash. Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre. articles.title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent
articles.description: The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black. “The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.” Continue reading...

articles.title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts
articles.description: Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way. I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me. Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. articles.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
articles.description: In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections. And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And

articles.title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
articles.description: The Russian film-maker spent 40 days in a coma and suffered 92% lung damage during the pandemic. He describes how making new movie Minotaur helped his rehabilitation Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.” Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma . He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step
articles.description: The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower? But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride , has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. articles.title: Country diary: It’s been a strange year for seasons – now our fungi are in disarray | Michael White
articles.description: Cranbrook, Kent: Some species are absent, some have appeared twice – this may be a hangover from the summer drought and ‘second spring’ As autumn intensifies, it is easy for surface-dwellers such as ourselves to forget that we have already seen the trees turn once this year – not from shortening days, but for want of water. Summer turned leaves and meadows brown, until heavy rain in September and a second “spring” painted green all signs of the drought here in Kent, and banished at a stroke our fleeting interest in it. Subterranean organisms, though, and those that span both worlds, have far longer memories. The boundary oak between the lower paddocks will now for ever have a narrow growth-ring within its girth, and fungi, to the human eye at least, have been sent into utter disarray. articles.description: Young’s abusers were convicted through suspect-centric prosecution, though much more needs to be done for victims Hope can be found in the darkest of places. Joanne Young stood outside Winchester crown court on Thursday and said she was relieved – not just for herself and her family – but for women in the future. Young, who was subjected to years of drugging and rape by her husband , who invited other men to assault her, waived her anonymity to speak out. Continue reading...

articles.title: Digested week: Pity the touring royals – and the hacks made to schlep around after them
articles.description: It’s a hard life for the Prince and Princess of Wales, but spare a thought too for jailed Bankman-Fried and the overlooked 007s All eyes on China ahead of the trilateral summit this week, but it’s India and the three-day royal tour by the Prince and Princess of Wales that catches my eye. The couple arrive in Mumbai and as a steady stream of photos emanates from their back-to-back schedule, the usual question surfaces: how on earth do they stand it? Continue reading...

articles.title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
articles.description: The actor’s new role as James Bond could be bad news for DC, as a new owner, new chief and new director already threaten to shake and stir Gotham’s distinctive hero Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007 . The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments. Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap , delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
articles.description: Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does . Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all. For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Super Bowl of F1: how Las Vegas GP has hit the jackpot after turbulent start
articles.description: George Russell calls it the biggest race on the Formula One calendar bar Monaco – and the numbers back him up That Formula One has achieved a palpable success in hosting a race in Las Vegas is impossible to ignore. Even with this year’s outing a dead rubber and with the city in perhaps its least flattering light, the cold drizzle of a Thursday afternoon beneath gunmetal-grey skies, the fans who have flocked to Nevada were irrepressibly enthusiastic. Long queues stretched out into the streets before the gates were even open and it seems many locals who were initially cool to the somewhat disruptive F1 circus have embraced the fans, their fervour for the sport and the positive impact of the race. Continue reading...

articles.title: Death threats to Bowens revealed after De Boinville security incident
articles.description: Abuse and threats are becoming a grimly familiar part of daily routine for riders, confirms jockeys’ association When Nico de Boinville received a security escort back to his car after racing at Plumpton on Monday, following a telephone threat to harm the jockey received at Nicky Henderson’s stable, it was the first time that such a move had received widespread media attention. It was not, however, the first time that it had been felt necessary to give a rider additional protection at a racecourse. James Bowen said on Friday, in a blog for the bookmaker Dragonsports, that he and his brother, Sean, the champion over jumps, “were both the subject of death threats” during a meeting at Ffos Las in October 2025, “to the extent that we had security accompanying us between the paddock and weighing room for the next three or four days.” Continue reading...

articles.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
articles.description: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. Continue reading...

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex
articles.description: Mayor plans to close jail by 2032 and relocate its remaining population to smaller facilities across four boroughs Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, with a goal to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population by the end of 2032. “It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane. This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146m in the evidence-based supports that helps break the cycles of incarceration.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Dmitri Kasterine obituary
articles.description: Photographer who captured the humanity of subjects including Queen Elizabeth II, Dirk Bogarde, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Tom Stoppard In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.” Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance. Continue reading...

It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. articles.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
articles.description: Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump says Vance’s statement blaming Iran war for Republican midterm wipeout was ‘fine’ in wide-ranging press conference – live
articles.description: US president again claims Republicans’ midterms losses were because he ‘wasn’t on the ballot’, vows to fight for datacenters and boasts of his relationship with Xi Jinping Sign up for the Breaking News US email We’re also following the latest on Capitol Hill as the battle for Senate majority leader between Democrats Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen plays out. We had a key update on Wednesday, when Elissa Slotkin , the influential senator from Michigan, pledged her support for Van Hollen, a progressive. While Slotkin had been vocal that she would not back Schumer in the secret-ballot election on 1 December, saying that she wanted to see change in party leadership as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress, until now she had not said whether Van Hollen had her vote. Continue reading...

articles.title: Expect a fearsome backlash from cornered All Blacks – but England must play with freedom | Ugo Monye
articles.description: New Zealand want to ease the pain of defeat by Wales but England’s squad depth will make them formidable opponents I’ve heard it said that in New Zealand, 65% of people are rugby fans but 95% are All Blacks fans. Regardless of how accurate those numbers are, the sentiment is clear, and it explains why Dave Rennie said his players had “let the country down” by losing to Wales. A backlash is coming at Twickenham. I spent some time with Kieran Read this week, one of the greatest All Blacks to play the game. He enjoyed some fine wins over England during his career but also suffered two defeats and clearly still carries those scars. The pain and anguish remain and, after last weekend’s chastening defeat in Cardiff , the All Blacks will be burning. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tom Brady in talks over buying Chelsea stake after Birmingham City exit
articles.description: NFL legend was Chelsea guest at Club World Cup Brady has good relationship with Behdad Eghbali Tom Brady is in discussions about buying a small stake in Chelsea. The NFL legend sold a minority share in Birmingham City this month after three years, a move sources said was to pave the way for investing at Stamford Bridge. Brady was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year and was seen celebrating with the players after their remarkable 3-0 final win over Paris Saint-Germain. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sandpaper and silence: Marsh hides away as England’s T20 winners roll into MCG
articles.description: Amid an increasingly febrile atmosphere in Australia, the Twenty20 captain is not expected at any press conferences After a toe-curling, stonewalling press conference before the recent one-day series against England, Australia’s usually happy-go-lucky T20 captain, Mitch Marsh, opted out of a repeat before the Twenty20s that start here on Saturday. In his place came Victoria’s Sam Harper to talk about his looming debut at the MCG. A nice local angle, for sure, with the 29-year-old wicketkeeper having overcome some troubling concussions in the past. But also a touch optimistic if intended to switch the focus in Australia away from the sandpaper skip fire. Continue reading...

articles.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
articles.description: The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems Continue reading...

articles.title: Bring in ‘cosmetic cowboys’ law to avoid more deaths, says family of butt lift victim
articles.description: Relatives speak out as inquest jury finds Alice Webb’s death after filler entered her organs was accidental The family of a woman who died after a botched Brazilian butt lift have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people lose their lives. Speaking as an inquest jury concluded Alice Webb’s death was accidental, her family said they were astonished people were still having BBLs despite what had happened to her. Continue reading...

articles.title: Mahmood ‘smells a rat’ over housing provision for vulnerable people in Birmingham
articles.description: Warnings over exploitation risks come amid push for investigation into supported exempt accommodation sector The home secretary has launched an attack on providers of housing for vulnerable residents in her Birmingham constituency, saying she “smells a rat” after warnings over spiralling costs and risks of exploitation. A push for an independent investigation into the supported exempt accommodation (SEA) sector in Birmingham, one of the largest in the country, is under way. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
articles.description: Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset. Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory. Continue reading...
